A monopsony is a market with only one buyer and many sellers. That single buyer holds the pricing power, so it can push the price it pays down below what a competitive market would give. The classic example is a company town where one employer is the only place to work, so it can set wages. It's the mirror image of a monopoly, which is one seller and many buyers.

[[GIST]] one buyer, many sellers

Entropy is really a **count of arrangements**. Picture four coins: all heads has just one arrangement, but two heads and two tails has six. So the second state has higher entropy, because more arrangements produce the same thing you see. That's it. High entropy means many underlying configurations look identical from the outside, and systems drift that way simply because there are so many more of those arrangements, not because they're getting messier.

[[GIST]] entropy counts arrangements, not mess

The lecturer's right, and the correct reading is the other way round: a p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as yours, **assuming the null hypothesis is true**. So it's a statement about the data given the null, not about the null given the data. The common mistake is flipping that conditional, which is why a small p-value doesn't mean the null is probably false, only that the data would be unlikely if it were.

[[GIST]] p-value is data given null, not reverse

Because each round of spending is smaller than the last, and those rounds add up to a finite total. If I spend a dollar, the recipient spends 80 cents of it, the next person spends 80 percent of that, and so on. That's a geometric series: 1 + 0.8 + 0.8² + 0.8³ and so on. The sum of that series is 1 divided by (1 minus 0.8), which is 5. So the multiplier isn't a coincidence, it's just the total of all those shrinking rounds of re-spending.

[[GIST]] shrinking rounds sum to five

The lecturer is making a **revisionist** point, and it's a defensible one. The treaties of 1648 were about ending the Thirty Years' War and settling specific grievances, imperial rights, and confessional boundaries. They didn't announce a general doctrine of sovereignty. The familiar reading, that Westphalia created a system of equal, sovereign, territorially bounded states, was largely built up later, and nineteenth-century jurists and international lawyers had a stake in that story because it gave their own field a founding moment. So the useful move is to ask what the treaties actually say versus what later writers needed them to say.

[[GIST]] Westphalia myth, later lawyers' framing

Start from a portfolio that's long one option and short delta units of the stock, so its value is Π = V − ΔS. Over a small step dt, the stock follows dS = μS dt + σS dW, and Ito's lemma gives dV = (∂V/∂t + μS ∂V/∂S + ½σ²S² ∂²V/∂S²) dt + σS ∂V/∂S dW. Pick Δ = ∂V/∂S so the dW terms cancel, leaving dΠ = (∂V/∂t + ½σ²S² ∂²V/∂S²) dt. That portfolio is now riskless, so it must earn the risk-free rate, dΠ = rΠ dt = r(V − S ∂V/∂S) dt. Setting the two equal and rearranging gives ∂V/∂t + ½σ²S² ∂²V/∂S² + rS ∂V/∂S − rV = 0.

Two things are going on. Taxes and imports are **leakages**: a slice of each extra dollar leaves the domestic spending chain before it gets re-spent, so less of it becomes someone else's income. Taxes go to the government, imports go abroad, and neither one comes back as the next round of domestic consumption, so the chain dies out faster and the multiplier shrinks.

Real-world estimates come in lower for the same reason, plus a few more. The simple formula assumes every dollar gets spent at the same rate forever, but in reality people save more of a windfall, some spending leaks into imports, and the economy is already near full capacity, so extra demand partly shows up as higher prices rather than more output. Crowding out and interest-rate rises work the same way.

With a 25 percent income tax, the effective MPC becomes 0.8 times 0.75, which is 0.6, so the multiplier is 1 divided by 0.4, which is **2.5**.

[[GIST]] leakages shrink the multiplier to 2.5

A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the forward and reverse paths by the same amount, so it speeds both directions equally and the system still settles at the same equilibrium position. For the reverse reaction, it lowers that barrier too, by the same amount as the forward one. And it can't drive a non-spontaneous reaction because it changes only the kinetics, not the thermodynamics. If the free energy change is positive, no catalyst changes that, it just gets you to the same unfavorable place faster.

The theorem holds only when transaction costs are zero and bargaining is costless, which is why it's a benchmark rather than a description. Once you add real costs, who holds the right absolutely changes the outcome, because the party with the right starts from a different threat point and the surplus gets eaten by negotiation, enforcement, and holdout. So the useful move is to ask which specific friction is doing the work: information asymmetry, many parties, or the inability to write a complete contract. That's what tells you whether the right should sit with the polluter, the victim, or a regulator.

[[GIST]] zero transaction costs, so rarely real

It just writes 99 into that third slot, overwriting the 3 that x still points at. So x becomes `[1 2 99]`, and y now has length 3. A heap is optimized for one thing: getting the min or max in constant time, with insert and extract in O(log n). It's a partial order, so a parent is only guaranteed to beat its children, which is why you can't search it efficiently. A BST keeps a full ordering, so search, insert, and delete are all O(log n) and you can do ordered traversal, range queries, and find predecessors and successors. So if I need a priority queue, a heap. If I need ordered lookups or sorted iteration, a BST, and a balanced one like a red-black or AVL tree to keep that log n guarantee.

[[GIST]] heap for priority, BST for ordering

Clock keeps the frames in a circle, one **use bit** per frame, set by hardware on every reference. The hand starts at frame 0, empty frames fill from frame 0 upward, and a page arrives with its use bit already at 1. On a fault, look at the frame under the hand: if its bit is 1, clear it and move on; if it's 0, evict that page, load the new one with use 1, and step the hand to the next frame. A hit just sets the use bit back to 1, and the hand doesn't move.

Now the string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3 with 3 frames:

1. 7 faults into empty frame 0, use 1; hand moves to frame 1.
2. 0 faults into frame 1, use 1; hand to frame 2.
3. 1 faults into frame 2, use 1; hand to frame 0. Frames are 7, 0, 1.
4. 2 faults. The hand clears 7, 0, 1 and returns to frame 0, whose bit now reads 0, so it evicts 7, loads 2, use 1; hand to frame 1.
5. 0 is a hit in frame 1, use set to 1.
6. 3 faults. The hand clears frame 1's bit and moves on, finds frame 2's bit already 0, evicts 1, loads 3; hand to frame 0.
7. 0 is a hit in frame 1, use back to 1.
8. 4 faults. The hand clears 2, 0, 3, returns to frame 0 with bit 0, evicts 2, loads 4; hand to frame 1.
9. 2 faults. The hand finds frame 1's 0 with bit 0, evicts it, loads 2; hand to frame 2.
10. 3 is a hit in frame 2, use set to 1.

So the faults land on 7, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 2: **7 faults** total, which is the number the slide gives.

[[GIST]] hand clears 1s, evicts 0s, 7 faults

1. Tourists pay more because their demand is **less elastic**. The Lerner check shows it: for tourists (70 - 20)/70 = 0.714, so |Ed| = 1.4, while for commuters (40 - 20)/40 = 0.5, so |Ed| = 2. Since you set MR = MC in each market, the group that's less price-sensitive carries the higher price.

Amounts are signed (debits positive, credits negative). Postgres can't sum a group in a CHECK, so a **deferrable constraint trigger** on postings checks each entry sums to zero at commit. Add a unique key on **(entry_id, account_id)** and a trigger blocking edits once posted.

```sql
accounts(id PK, name, type, currency);

entries(id PK, occurred_at timestamptz, memo text);

postings(
  id PK,
  entry_id FK REFERENCES entries,
  account_id FK REFERENCES accounts,
  amount numeric(20,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount <> 0),
  currency text NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (entry_id, account_id)
);

CREATE CONSTRAINT TRIGGER balance_check
  AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON postings
  DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION assert_entry_balanced();
-- assert_entry_balanced: SUM(amount) per entry_id must equal 0
```

[[GIST]] signed postings, deferred balance trigger

Quicksort goes quadratic when the pivot splits the array badly every time, like always picking the smallest or largest element, so each partition peels off one item and you get n levels of work instead of log n. Sorted or reverse-sorted input with a first-or-last pivot is the classic trigger. Real implementations avoid it by choosing the pivot better, median-of-three or a random element, and by switching to insertion sort on small subarrays. Introsort adds a depth counter and falls back to heapsort if recursion gets too deep, which guarantees O(n log n) worst case. Three-way partitioning also helps a lot when there are many duplicate keys.

[[GIST]] bad pivots cause quadratic, randomization and introsort fix it

Brute force is to fix each starting index i, walk j forward accumulating the running sum, and check after each step whether it equals k, keeping the longest j minus i plus 1 that matches. It's correct because every contiguous subarray is exactly some pair i, j, so checking all of them can't miss the answer. That's O(n²) time and O(1) extra space, and it's slow because for each of the n starts we rescan up to n elements.

The optimal approach is a prefix-sum hash map. Let prefix[i] be the sum of the first i elements. A subarray from i to j sums to k exactly when prefix[j+1] minus prefix[i] equals k, so for each position we look up whether prefix[j+1] minus k has been seen before, and if so the length is the current index minus that stored index. We store the earliest index for each prefix sum, and seed the map with 0 mapped to index minus one so subarrays starting at the beginning are handled. That's O(n) time and O(n) space.

A sliding window does not work here. The usual window trick relies on the sum being monotonic as you move the boundaries, which holds for non-negative numbers, but with negatives adding an element can decrease the sum and shrinking can increase it, so you can't decide whether to advance the right edge or the left edge. The prefix-sum map is what handles that.

[[GIST]] prefix-sum map beats sliding window with negatives

No, it's at-least-once, not exactly-once. The relay polls unpublished rows every 250 ms in batches of up to 500, ordered by created_at, publishes them, then sets published_at. If it publishes a batch and crashes before it sets published_at, that batch gets published again on restart, so duplicates are expected. What actually removes them is consumer-side dedupe: each consumer records processed event_id values in a dedupe table inside the same transaction as its own side effects, kept for 7 days. So the guarantee is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers, not a single publish.

[[GIST]] at-least-once, dedupe on event_id

I'd split it into three stages so each one is independently retryable. First, a snapshot stage that freezes the day's ledger entries into a settlement run with a run ID, so nothing downstream reads a moving table. Second, a per-grower aggregation stage that computes each payout from that frozen set, sharded by grower so it parallelizes and a single grower's failure doesn't take down the batch. Third, a submission stage that sends the bank file and records the acknowledgement.

For rerun safety, the whole thing keys on the run ID and is idempotent. Each grower's payout row is written with a unique key on run ID plus grower, so recomputing overwrites rather than double-pays. The bank submission carries an idempotency key per payout, and I only mark a payout as sent after the bank's ack comes back, so a crash mid-send means the rerun resends and the bank dedupes. I'd also make the run resumable: it tracks which shards completed, so a rerun picks up the unfinished ones instead of redoing everything.

What I page on is the things that threaten the deadline or the money. The batch not starting at 02:00, the run not finishing with enough buffer before banks open, any grower whose payout fails to reconcile against the ledger, and a bank submission that errors or never acks. Reconciliation mismatches page immediately because that's a correctness problem, not just a latency one.

[[GIST]] snapshot, aggregate, submit; idempotent reruns; page on deadline and reconciliation

I'd run a consensus layer, something like etcd or Patroni, as the source of truth for who's primary. Each node heartbeats to the leader; if the primary misses its lease, the leader marks it down and promotes the replica with the least replication lag, so we don't lose acknowledged writes. Clients never hardcode the primary, they go through a proxy or a DNS name that the consensus layer repoints. And I'd set synchronous replication to at least one replica, so a write isn't acknowledged until it's on two nodes.

Split brain is exactly what the consensus layer prevents. A node only acts as primary if it holds the lease from the quorum, so a partitioned old primary loses its lease and demotes itself or gets fenced. With two replicas plus the primary, quorum is three of four, so a minority partition can never elect a second primary.

For a stream, I'd keep the sweep's state instead of rebuilding it. Two heaps: a min-heap of active holds keyed by end time, and a max-heap of pending holds keyed by start. On each insert, pop expired holds off the active heap, then push the new one. Cancels are a lazy delete, so I mark the id and drop it when it surfaces. That keeps each update O(log n) and the peak current without a full re-sweep.

[[GIST]] heaps, lazy delete, O(log n) per update
